Family Health

When breast-cancer risk runs in a family

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A family history of breast cancer can raise understandable questions about your own risk. Some cancers are linked to inherited gene variants, but having a variant does not make cancer inevitable. The useful next step is a careful assessment of your history and the test that could answer your particular question.

Genetic changes are not always inherited changes

Cancer develops as cells acquire changes that interfere with normal growth and control. Genes contain instructions for proteins involved in these processes, including repairing damaged DNA. A genetic change found in a breast tumour may have developed during the person’s life rather than having been inherited from a parent.

An inherited, or germline, variant is present from conception and can be passed through a family. Roughly 5–10% of breast cancers are often described as hereditary; current American Cancer Society information puts the proportion at up to 10%. Most cases therefore are not explained by a known inherited high-risk variant. A family cluster can also reflect shared risks or genetic factors that a current test does not fully identify.

Everyone has BRCA genes; harmful variants are what matter

BRCA1 and BRCA2 normally help cells repair DNA. Everyone has these genes. A harmful, or pathogenic, variant can reduce that protection and increase the chance that additional cellular changes lead to cancer. Carrying a variant means increased susceptibility, not that cancer is already present or will certainly develop.

Risk estimates depend on the gene, age, family history and study. CDC describes about 50 in 100 women with a BRCA variant developing breast cancer by age 70, while NCI describes a lifetime risk above 60% for harmful BRCA1 or BRCA2 variants. These use different time horizons and should not be treated as interchangeable personal predictions. A genetics professional can explain the estimate relevant to you.

The implications can extend beyond female breast cancer

Harmful BRCA variants can increase ovarian cancer risk, including related fallopian-tube and primary peritoneal cancers. They can also matter for pancreatic and prostate cancer. Breast cancer risk in men is increased, particularly with BRCA2, although BRCA1 can also be relevant. An inherited variant can pass through either side of a family, including relatives who never develop breast cancer.

Not every proposed association is equally established. Some research has suggested a link with melanoma, but the evidence is uncertain. NCI’s detailed review finds insufficient evidence to assume increased colorectal cancer risk from BRCA1 or BRCA2 alone. Bowel or skin-cancer screening should therefore reflect the full personal and family history rather than an automatic assumption that every cancer risk rises in the same way.

Other genes have their own cancer patterns

CDH1 is associated with hereditary diffuse gastric cancer and an increased risk of lobular breast cancer. PALB2 produces a protein that works with BRCA2 in DNA repair. Harmful PALB2 variants can substantially increase breast-cancer risk, but the result needs gene-specific interpretation.

PTEN helps regulate cell growth. Harmful variants can cause PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome, which includes Cowden syndrome and a tendency to certain benign growths and cancers. TP53 is involved in preventing damaged cells from continuing to grow; harmful variants can cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, with risks that can include breast cancer, brain tumours and other cancers.

These examples do not make every change in any of these genes harmful. Laboratories classify variants, and an uncertain finding is different from a pathogenic one. Testing and follow-up should match the particular gene and family pattern rather than applying one BRCA plan to every result.

Understand the often-quoted PALB2 risk number

A 2014 study of families with PALB2 mutations reported a 9.47-fold relative risk in one statistical model, compared with breast-cancer incidence in the UK during 1993–1997. That model assumed the same relative risk across ages. The study also examined how estimates varied with age and family history.

The number does not mean a 9.47% chance of cancer, a 47.9-fold risk, or a prediction that applies identically to every carrier today. Relative risk compares groups; absolute risk asks how many people develop cancer over a defined time. Ask for an age-specific absolute estimate and an explanation of uncertainty before using a research number to make decisions.

Build a history from both sides of the family

Useful details include several relatives with breast cancer, breast cancer diagnosed before age 50, ovarian cancer, male breast cancer, one person with both breast and ovarian cancer, or a known harmful variant in a relative. Pancreatic cancer and certain prostate cancers can also be relevant. Record the cancer type and age at diagnosis where possible.

Include your father’s side as well as your mother’s. A harmful BRCA variant can be inherited from either parent. If you carry one, each child has a 50% chance of inheriting that variant; that is not the child’s percentage chance of developing cancer. Each pregnancy is a separate inheritance event.

A small family, limited information, adoption or relatives dying young from other causes can make a pattern less obvious. Lack of a striking family history does not automatically rule out an inherited risk. If a relative has a test report, its exact gene and variant are more useful than a remembered description of a “positive cancer test”.

Testing is not reserved for a strong family history

A genetics assessment can be useful for someone who has cancer as well as someone who is currently well. For a person with breast cancer, inherited testing may influence treatment, future screening or risk-reduction decisions. Eligibility can depend on diagnosis, age, tumour features, ancestry and treatment options as well as family history.

For example, the 2024 ASCO–Society of Surgical Oncology guideline recommends offering BRCA1/2 testing to newly diagnosed breast-cancer patients aged 65 or younger, and to selected older patients based on their circumstances. This is a recommendation for people with a diagnosis, not a rule that everyone under 65 needs population screening.

Local services and later guidance may use different pathways. Ask your oncology or genetics team which test is appropriate and why. When investigating an unexplained family pattern, testing a relative who has had cancer first is often more informative, if that person is available and wishes to be tested.

What a blood or saliva test can and cannot show

A germline test usually uses blood or saliva. The laboratory looks for specified inherited variants or examines a panel of relevant genes. A BRCA-only test does not check every cancer-risk gene, but modern testing is not necessarily limited to BRCA1 and BRCA2. The best scope depends on the clinical question and any known family result.

A tumour test examines changes in cancer cells and may sometimes suggest an inherited variant, but it does not replace germline testing. A separate sample may be needed to clarify inheritance. Some consumer tests examine only a limited set of variants; a negative result from such a test is not a comprehensive all-clear.

Before testing, ask what genes and types of changes are included, what the possible results mean and who will help interpret them. The sample collection may be simple, but the decision and interpretation can be complex. A test cannot measure every environmental, hormonal or lifestyle factor affecting breast-cancer risk.

Positive, negative and uncertain results mean different things

A pathogenic or likely pathogenic result identifies a harmful variant and can guide a personalised plan. It does not establish that you currently have cancer or tell exactly whether or when you will develop it. Relatives may be offered testing for the same variant.

A negative result is most informative when a known family variant was specifically tested for and was not found. If no familial cause has been identified, a negative panel may be uninformative: your history can still justify additional screening. Even a true negative does not reduce all cancer risk to zero.

A variant of uncertain significance, or VUS, means there is not enough evidence to classify the change as harmful or benign. It should not by itself drive preventive surgery or be treated like a positive pathogenic result. Base care on established risks and arrange a way to receive updates if the laboratory later reclassifies it.

Testing children depends on the particular syndrome

Predictive BRCA1/2 testing is generally not recommended before age 18 because routine BRCA risk-reduction measures are aimed at adults and associated childhood cancers are very uncommon. Families can still discuss how and when to share information in an age-appropriate way.

That advice must not be extended to every inherited cancer condition. In Li-Fraumeni syndrome, for example, surveillance can begin in infancy, so at-risk children may be offered TP53 testing. A cancer-genetics team should decide what is relevant to the child and the specific family variant.

Make the result part of a supported care plan

Depending on the result and overall risk, options may include earlier or additional screening, preventive medicines or risk-reducing surgery. None is an automatic requirement for everyone with a gene change. Discuss benefits, limitations, timing, fertility or family plans and your own priorities with the appropriate specialists.

Testing can bring relief, uncertainty or anxiety about yourself and relatives. Genetic counselling provides space to consider these reactions as well as medical decisions. Ask about costs, privacy and who will receive the result under your local arrangements before proceeding. Keep a copy of the report and an agreed follow-up plan.

Report a new breast lump, nipple change or other concerning symptom promptly rather than waiting for genetic testing. Inherited-risk testing is not a substitute for assessing a current symptom. You can ask for risk advice even if you are not ready to have a test.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Inherited susceptibility differs from a genetic change found only in a tumour.

Testing eligibility and care depend on the specific gene, diagnosis and family history; uncertain variants are not treated as established harmful results.

How BeMama can help

Write down cancer types, ages at diagnosis and known genetic reports from both sides of your family before an appointment.

When to seek help

A negative genetic result does not rule out breast cancer. Seek assessment for new breast symptoms and do not make preventive-surgery decisions from a VUS or an unconfirmed consumer result.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Most breast cancers are not due to a known inherited high-risk variant.
  • BRCA genes normally protect DNA; harmful variants increase susceptibility.
  • Both sides of the family and several cancer types can matter.
  • A risk percentage needs a defined population and time horizon.
  • Genetic counselling helps turn a result into an individual plan.

Frequently asked questions

Is every breast cancer inherited?

No. Cancer involves genetic changes, but many arise during life rather than being inherited. A minority of breast cancers are explained by known hereditary susceptibility.

Does a harmful BRCA result mean I will definitely get cancer?

No. It increases risk but does not determine whether or when cancer will occur. Screening and risk-reduction choices are individual.

Does my father’s family history count?

Yes. BRCA and other relevant variants can pass through either parent. Include cancers on both sides of the family.

Does 50% inheritance mean a child has a 50% cancer risk?

No. The 50% figure is the chance of inheriting a parent’s variant in each pregnancy. Cancer risk depends on the gene and other factors.

Does PALB2 mean a fixed 9.47-fold risk for everyone?

No. That figure came from one model in a 2014 family study. Personal counselling should use age-specific absolute risks, family history and current evidence.

Can testing be useful without a strong family history?

Yes. A personal cancer diagnosis, age, tumour features, ancestry or treatment choices may justify testing. Discuss the criteria that apply to your situation.

Does a blood or saliva test look at every cancer gene?

Not necessarily. Some tests target a known variant or BRCA alone; others examine several genes. Check the scope before interpreting a result.

Is a variant of uncertain significance a positive result?

It is not a confirmed harmful finding. It should not by itself determine preventive surgery. Your team can explain follow-up and possible later reclassification.

Should children have predictive BRCA testing?

Usually not before age 18. Other cancer syndromes, such as Li-Fraumeni syndrome, can require childhood testing because care begins earlier; ask a genetics team.

Can I ignore a new lump after a negative genetic test?

No. Genetic testing does not diagnose or exclude a current breast problem. Have new symptoms assessed even when no harmful inherited variant was found.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
